name: Invisalign attachments / chewies

card.summary: Small bonded bumps and rubbery bite cylinders that help clear aligners grip and seat; useful accessories with little dedicated research.
card.note: Attachments are placed by a clinician; chewies are an adjunct, and aligners overall have limits for some movements.

quick.overview:
Clear aligners are plastic trays that move teeth in stages. Two accessories come up constantly: attachments, which are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to teeth, and chewies, soft cylinders users bite on to press the tray fully onto the teeth.

Attachments are part of the treatment plan set by the clinician. Chewies are mostly discussed by patients as a way to help trays seat; sources reviewed give no dedicated trial of them.
quick.mechanism: Because plastic is less rigid than metal, attachments give the tray something to push against so it can rotate or pull down teeth. Chewies work by biting force pressing the tray against the teeth to close small gaps.
quick.risks: More attachments can make the aligners look less discreet. Aligners in general are considered less effective than braces for rotations, extrusion and front-to-back jaw discrepancies, and relapse is reported.

lead: Attachments and chewies are two accessories of clear aligner treatment that help straighten teeth, which is how they improve a smile and the look of the lower face. Attachments are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to certain teeth by the clinician; they give the plastic tray something to push against so it can rotate or pull down teeth, since plastic is less rigid than metal.[1] Chewies are soft cylinders that wearers bite on to press a new tray fully onto the teeth, an informal accessory discussed mostly by patients.

Clear aligners typically move teeth about 0.25 to 0.33 mm per stage, are worn around 22 hours a day, and treatment averages about 13.5 months.[1] Studies of Invisalign with attachments have measured upper-arch expansion in adolescents and adults,[2][3][4] and a laboratory study compared how different attachment shapes control premolar rotation.[5] A 2014 systematic review found study quality insufficient to determine effectiveness of aligners overall, and aligners are considered less effective than conventional braces for rotations, extrusion and jaw discrepancies.[1]
infobox: Soft bite cylinders for seating trays

paras: Attachments are bonded by a clinician to selected teeth. More attachments can make aligners less aesthetically pleasing.[1] Their shapes vary; a laboratory comparison of 11 attachment designs and a no-attachment setup on a premolar found that vertical rectangular attachments generated the highest derotational moment but also the most side effects such as intrusive force, torque and tipping.[5] Attachment resin is a composite: a randomized trial examined surface wear of two composites on 40 attachments over six months of clinical use.[6]
Chewies are used by the wearer at home. Commercial listings describe them as silicone or rubber cylinders bitten on after inserting a tray, and they are commonly discussed on patient forums.

Align Technology, maker of Invisalign, was founded in 1997 by Zia Chishti, with US sales beginning in 1999. Orthodontists were initially resistant, but consumers embraced the product, and 80,000 dentists had been trained by 2014.[1]

Aligners are likely useful for moderate front-teeth crowding but less effective than braces for rotations, extrusion and front-back jaw discrepancies, and relapse of front teeth has been reported more often. They are not recommended for children.[1] A nightly retainer is usually advised after treatment.[1]

In studies using Invisalign with attachments as the only auxiliaries, a prospective series of 28 adults examined maxillary expansion,[4] a 28-patient study of mean age 17 evaluated the efficacy and accuracy of expansion against the planned virtual models,[2] and a prospective study of 23 children aged about 9 examined upper-arch width with the Invisalign First system.[3]

A 2026 questionnaire study of 124 parents of children and adolescents in clear aligner treatment rated several compliance indicators; chewies usage scored lowest of the indicators, at 3.21 out of 5, below appointment adherence and timely aligner change.[7]

No completed controlled trial of chewies has been published to the knowledge of this wiki's sources. A registered randomized trial at the University of Baghdad (NCT07726485, 34 adults, started February 2026) compares routine seater use with additional daily bedtime use, with predictability of tooth movement at four months as the primary outcome; it is listed as active, not recruiting.[8] Studies of attachments are described above and cover composite wear, expansion accuracy and laboratory force systems.[2][3][4][5][6]

timeline.event: Align Technology founded by Zia Chishti [1].
Randomized trial of aligner seaters (chewies) begins at the University of Baghdad.[8]

angle.text: Attachments let clear aligners make the rotations and vertical movements that straighten a smile, and chewies are used by patients to help each new tray seat. Straight, even teeth are a visible part of facial attractiveness, and aligners are less noticeable than braces.
